modules.lesson_html:
The core idea

In 2015 Google's Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems made one picture famous: a tiny box labelled "ML code" surrounded by much bigger boxes — configuration, data collection, feature extraction, data verification, serving infrastructure, monitoring, process management. The point: most of the cost and risk of an ML system lives outside the model.

Debt patterns you must be able to name

  • Entanglement (CACE) — Changing Anything Changes Everything. Features interact, so adding, removing or rescaling one input can shift the whole model's behaviour. You cannot make isolated improvements.
  • Correction cascades — model B is trained on model A's output to "fix" a new case. Now improving A can break B.
  • Undeclared consumers — other systems silently read your predictions or log files. You change the model; their behaviour changes; nobody knows why.
  • Unstable data dependencies — an input signal owned by another team changes meaning or distribution without notice.
  • Underutilised data dependencies — features that add almost nothing but still add breakage risk (legacy, bundled, epsilon features).
  • Feedback loops — direct (the model picks the data it learns from, like a recommender) and hidden (two systems influence each other through the world). Pricing models are especially prone: your predicted price shifts seller behaviour, which shifts future prices.
  • Glue code and pipeline jungles — large amounts of code exist only to move data in and out of generic packages; pipelines grow by accretion.
  • Dead experimental codepaths and configuration debt — configuration often outgrows code and is rarely tested.

Rules of ML worth memorising

From Martin Zinkevich's Rules of Machine Learning (Google): - Rule #1: Don't be afraid to launch a product without ML. - Rule #4: Keep the first model simple and get the infrastructure right. - Rule #5: Test the infrastructure independently from the ML. - Rule #29: The best way to make sure you train like you serve is to save the set of features used at serving time and pipe them to a log for training. - Rule #32: Re-use code between your training pipeline and serving pipeline.

How a staff engineer uses this

When you review a system, walk the "boxes" around the ML code and ask, for each: who owns it, how is it tested, what happens when it silently changes? That question list is your review template for the capstone.

modules.lesson_html:
Training-serving skew

Skew is any difference between what the model saw in training and what it sees in production. Three root causes: 1. Code skew — features computed by different code paths (a Spark job for training, a Python function at serving). 2. Data skew — the serving data distribution differs from training (often a symptom of a pipeline bug, not real-world drift). 3. Time skew / leakage — training rows used information that would not have been available at prediction time.

Point-in-time correctness

When you join features to labels for training, each feature value must be the value as of the label's timestamp, never later. Getting this wrong is label leakage: offline metrics look great, production performance collapses. A point-in-time (as-of) join is the fix; feature stores automate it.

Feature stores

A feature store gives you: one feature definition used for both training and serving; an offline store (history, for training via point-in-time joins); an online store (latest values, low latency, for serving); and materialisation jobs that keep them consistent. Uber's Michelangelo popularised this; Feast is the main open-source option. A feature store is worth it when several models share features or need low-latency online lookups — not for a single batch model.

Data contracts

A data contract is an explicit, versioned agreement between a data producer and consumers: schema, types, nullability, allowed ranges, semantics, freshness SLA, and an owner. The key design question is where it is enforced: - at the producer (best — bad data never lands), - at ingestion into your pipeline (good — fail fast), - at training/serving time (last line of defence). Contracts should fail loudly in CI and in pipelines, and changes should go through versioning (additive changes are safe; renames and type changes are breaking).

Contract propagation

Your MLOps-Toolbox idea of propagating contracts from data → features → model → API is exactly the staff-level move: the model signature becomes a contract that serving validates against, so a schema change upstream fails a build, not a customer request.

modules.lesson_html:
The ML Test Score

Breck et al. (Google) proposed 28 tests in four groups — data, model development, infrastructure, and monitoring — with a final score taken as the minimum of the four group scores. Using the minimum is deliberate: a system is only as ready as its weakest area. Examples: feature expectations are captured in a schema; model staleness impact is known; the full pipeline is integration-tested; models can be rolled back; training and serving features are checked for skew.

MLOps maturity (Google's levels)

  • Level 0 — manual, notebook-driven, rare releases, no monitoring.
  • Level 1 — automated training pipeline with continuous training (CT), data and model validation inside the pipeline, a model registry.
  • Level 2 — CI/CD of the pipeline itself: pipeline code is tested, built and deployed automatically. Key distinction: in ML you deploy a pipeline that produces models, not just a model.

Release strategies

  • Shadow — new model receives a copy of live traffic; predictions are logged but not used. Zero user risk; validates latency, errors and prediction distribution. Cannot measure business impact.
  • Canary — a small percentage of real traffic uses the new model; expand if healthy. Real impact on a few users; fast rollback.
  • A/B test — randomised split to measure causal business impact with statistical power. Slow; needs enough traffic.
  • Blue-green — two full environments; switch all traffic at once; instant rollback but no gradual exposure.
  • Interleaving / bandits — common for ranking; out of scope here.

Release gates

A gate is an automated check that blocks promotion: schema checks, offline metric thresholds vs the champion, slice-level checks (no segment regresses by more than X), latency and size budgets, and — for LLM systems — eval scores (Pillar 4). Gates must compare against the current champion, not a fixed number, or the bar slowly drifts down.

modules.lesson_html:
Kinds of change

  • Data (covariate) drift — P(X) changes: input distribution shifts (more flood-damaged cars after a storm).
  • Prediction drift — the distribution of model outputs shifts. Often the earliest signal you can see.
  • Concept drift — P(Y|X) changes: the relationship itself changes (same car, different price because the market moved). Only detectable with labels or proxies.
  • Label shift — P(Y) changes.

Metrics

  • PSI (Population Stability Index) — common in finance; rough guide: <0.1 no significant change, 0.1–0.25 moderate, >0.25 significant.
  • KS test, Wasserstein distance, Jensen-Shannon divergence for numeric features; chi-squared for categoricals.
  • Caution: with large samples, statistical tests flag tiny, irrelevant shifts as "significant". Prefer effect-size metrics with thresholds tuned on history.

What to monitor (in priority order)

  1. Service health — latency, errors, throughput (standard SRE).
  2. Data quality — nulls, schema, ranges, freshness (cheapest, catches most incidents).
  3. Prediction distribution — drift in outputs.
  4. Model quality — once labels arrive (for auctions: when the hammer price is known), compute real error by segment.
  5. Business KPIs — sell-through, margin.

SLOs and incidents

An SLO is a target on a user-visible indicator (e.g. 99.5% of pricing requests return in <300 ms; weekly MAPE on settled auctions < X%). The error budget is the allowed failure; spending it fast triggers action. Your public-holiday pricing incident is a classic: a calendar effect the model had not seen → good postmortem material. Postmortems are blameless and end with owned, dated actions.

modules.lesson_html:
What an eval is

An eval is a test for an AI system: an input/task, the system's output (or full transcript), and grading logic. Graders come in three kinds: code-based (assertions, regex, schema checks, exact match, unit tests on generated code), model-based (LLM-as-judge), and human. Prefer code where possible: cheap, fast, deterministic.

Three levels (Hamel Husain's framing)

  1. Unit tests / assertions — run on every change; cheap.
  2. Human and model evaluation — on sampled traces; periodic.
  3. A/B testing — real users; for significant changes.

Error analysis is the core skill

Before writing any metric, look at your data: 1. Collect 50–100+ real or realistic traces. 2. Open coding — read each, write free-text notes on what went wrong. Focus on the first upstream failure in a trace. 3. Axial coding — group notes into a small set of failure categories (e.g. "wrong auction date", "ignores lot condition", "replies in English to a BM question", "hallucinated fee"). 4. Count them. Fix the obvious ones directly (prompt or code); build evals for the persistent, important ones. 5. Repeat as the product changes. Generic metrics like "helpfulness 1–5" or off-the-shelf "faithfulness" scores rarely track what actually breaks in your product.

Datasets

  • Start from real traces; add synthetic inputs by varying dimensions (persona × feature × scenario) — generate inputs, not expected outputs.
  • Keep provenance and version datasets like code.
  • Separate capability evals (can it do hard new things — expected pass rate lower) from regression evals (it used to work — expected ~100%).

Binary beats scales

Pass/fail judgments with a written critique are more reliable and actionable than 1–5 scales, where nobody agrees what a "3" means.

modules.lesson_html:
Why judges need validation

An LLM judge is itself a model making predictions. Zheng et al. (MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena) showed strong judges can agree with humans at levels similar to human-human agreement — but also documented biases: - Position bias — favouring the first (or second) answer in pairwise comparisons. Mitigate by swapping order and requiring consistency. - Verbosity bias — preferring longer answers. - Self-enhancement bias — favouring outputs from the same model family. - Limited ability to grade maths/reasoning it can't do itself.

Critique shadowing (Hamel Husain)

  1. Find the principal domain expert (one person whose judgment defines "good").
  2. Build a diverse dataset of real and synthetic interactions.
  3. The expert gives pass/fail + a written critique for each.
  4. Fix obvious errors in the product first.
  5. Build the judge prompt using expert critiques as few-shot examples.
  6. Measure agreement with the expert on held-out data; iterate the prompt.
  7. Use error analysis to create narrower, specialised judges where needed.

Measure the judge like a classifier

Treat expert labels as ground truth. Split into train (few-shot examples), dev (iterate), and test (final report). Report: - TPR (true positive rate) — of truly passing outputs, how many the judge passes. - TNR (true negative rate) — of truly failing outputs, how many the judge fails. Raw accuracy hides problems when classes are imbalanced (e.g. 90% pass).

Correcting the pass rate

With known TPR and TNR, the observed judge pass rate p_obs can be corrected: p_true ≈ (p_obs + TNR − 1) / (TPR + TNR − 1). Example: TPR 0.9, TNR 0.8, observed 0.75 → (0.75 + 0.8 − 1)/(0.9 + 0.8 − 1) = 0.55/0.7 ≈ 0.79.

Criteria drift

Shankar et al. ("Who Validates the Validators?") found people's evaluation criteria change as they grade outputs — you discover what "good" means by looking. So judge building is iterative, and criteria must be re-checked when the product changes.

Practical rules

One judge per failure mode, binary output, ask for reasoning before the verdict, use a strong model, pin the judge model version, and re-validate after any judge-prompt or model change.

modules.lesson_html:
RAG: split the problem

  • Retrieval — did we fetch the right context? Metrics: recall@k, precision@k, MRR/nDCG against labelled relevant documents.
  • Generation — given the context, is the answer faithful/grounded (claims supported by context) and relevant/correct? Frameworks like RAGAS compute reference-free metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall) — useful starting points, but validate them against your own labels before trusting them.

Agents: transcript vs outcome

Anthropic's framing: the transcript is what the agent said and did; the outcome is the final state of the environment (was the booking made? does the code pass tests?). Grade outcomes where possible; grade transcripts for process requirements (did it ask for confirmation before a payment? did it call the right tool with valid arguments?).

What to evaluate in agents

  • Task success — outcome-based.
  • Tool use — correct tool selection, valid arguments, handling errors.
  • Trajectory — efficiency (steps, tokens, cost), loops, unnecessary calls.
  • Policy adherence — e.g. τ-bench tests agents interacting with simulated users under domain policies (retail, airline).
  • Safety — refuses out-of-policy actions; resists prompt injection from tool outputs.

Non-determinism

Run each task multiple times (trials). - pass@k — probability at least one of k attempts succeeds (capability). - pass^k — probability all k attempts succeed (reliability). τ-bench showed pass^k drops sharply as k grows — agents that "can" do a task often can't do it consistently. For production, reliability is what users feel.

Benchmarks vs product evals

Public benchmarks (SWE-bench, τ-bench, GAIA) tell you about models; they don't tell you about your product. Use them to shortlist models, then rely on your own evals.

modules.lesson_html:
Tracing

An LLM app trace is a tree of spans: request → retrieval → LLM call(s) → tool calls → response. OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions (still in development status — check the current version) standardise attributes like gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.provider.name, token usage, and agent/tool spans. Using the standard means any backend (Application Insights, Langfuse, Phoenix, Datadog…) can read your traces, and you avoid vendor lock-in. Capture prompts and completions only where privacy rules allow — the conventions say instrumentations must let you turn that off.

What to measure in production

  • Ops: latency (TTFT, total), errors, tokens and cost per request/team.
  • Quality: online evals on a sample (cheap assertions on 100%, LLM judges on a sample), user feedback (thumbs, edits, retries, abandonment).
  • Safety: guardrail triggers, PII detection, injection attempts.

Offline ↔ online loop

Production traces → sampled for review → error analysis → new eval cases → offline suite grows → release gate gets stronger. This flywheel is the single most valuable thing an AI platform can provide.

Eval-gated CI/CD

Treat prompts, model versions, retrieval configs and tool definitions as versioned artifacts. Any change triggers: 1. Fast assertions (seconds) on every commit. 2. Full offline suite (minutes) on PRs — compare to champion; fail if any critical slice regresses beyond a threshold, with confidence intervals for small sets. 3. Shadow or canary in production with online evals before full rollout. This is the LLM version of your champion-challenger gate (p1m3).

Guardrails

Input and output checks around the model (topic filters, PII, injection detectors, schema validation). They're part of the system — so evaluate their false-positive and false-negative rates too.

modules.lesson_html:
Why this is its own module

Most eval knowledge is English-first. Malaysian users code-switch within a sentence ("Boleh check tak bila auction start, I nak bid lori tu"), use Manglish particles (lah, kan, meh), and mix scripts. Models can look fine on English benchmarks and fail here — and few people in the world can evaluate it well. This is your differentiator.

Benchmarks to know

  • SEA-HELM (AI Singapore) — holistic SEA evaluation with five pillars: NLP classics, LLM-specifics, SEA linguistics, SEA culture, and safety; public leaderboard and open code.
  • MalayMMLU (Universiti Malaya × YTL AI Labs, EMNLP Findings 2024) — 24k+ multiple-choice questions across Malaysian school-curriculum subjects.
  • MyCulture (Universiti Malaya) — Malaysian culture knowledge with an open-ended format to reduce MCQ shortcuts. Limits: MCQ benchmarks test knowledge, not conversational behaviour; contamination risk; little coverage of colloquial code-switching.

Pitfalls of translated benchmarks

Machine-translated English sets carry translationese, lose cultural context (wrong holidays, names, prices in USD), and miss code-switching. Prefer native-authored items; if you translate, have native speakers review and localise.

Designing code-switching evals

Define dimensions and sample across them: - Language mix — pure BM, pure English, BM-English mix, Manglish, with Mandarin/Cantonese/Tamil terms. - Register — formal (customer complaint letter) vs casual (WhatsApp). - Task — Q&A, instruction following, extraction, refusal. Failure modes to check: language fidelity (replies in the user's language or mix?), comprehension of particles/slang, cultural correctness (local institutions, holidays, currency RM), and safety that still holds in BM (some guardrails are weaker in non-English).

Judges in other languages

LLM judges may be less reliable in BM/Manglish. Validate the judge per language slice with native-speaker labels and report TPR/TNR per slice.

modules.lesson_html:
Two phases

  • Prefill — process the whole prompt in parallel. Large matrix-matrix multiplies → compute-bound. Dominates time to first token (TTFT).
  • Decode — generate one token at a time per sequence. Each step must read all model weights from GPU memory to produce just one token per sequence → memory-bandwidth-bound at small batch sizes. Dominates time per output token (TPOT), a.k.a. inter-token latency.

The key back-of-envelope

At batch size 1, a decode step reads every weight once. A 7B model in FP16 is ~14 GB. On a GPU with ~2 TB/s memory bandwidth, the floor is roughly 14 GB / 2 TB/s ≈ 7 ms per token, no matter how many FLOPs the GPU has. Batching amortises that weight read across many sequences, which is why throughput rises with batch size until compute becomes the limit.

Arithmetic intensity

FLOPs per byte moved. Each GPU has a ratio (peak FLOPs / bandwidth). Below it you're memory-bound; above it, compute-bound. Decode at small batch is far below; prefill is above.

KV cache

To avoid recomputing attention over past tokens, each layer stores keys and values for every token. Size per token:

2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value

Example (Llama-2-7B-like: 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head_dim 128, FP16 = 2 bytes): 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 524,288 bytes ≈ 0.5 MB per token. A 4,096-token sequence ≈ 2 GB. KV cache — not weights — usually limits how many concurrent requests you can serve. Grouped-query attention (GQA) cuts KV heads (e.g. 8 instead of 32), shrinking the cache 4×.

Memory budget

GPU memory = weights + KV cache + activations/overhead. Weights: params × bytes (FP16 = 2, INT8 = 1, INT4 = 0.5). A 70B model in FP16 (~140 GB) doesn't fit on one 80 GB GPU → tensor parallelism across GPUs, or quantisation.

Metrics vocabulary

TTFT, TPOT/ITL, end-to-end latency = TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1), throughput (tokens/s across all users), goodput (throughput that meets the latency SLO).

modules.lesson_html:
Static vs continuous batching

Static batching waits for a batch, runs it until the longest sequence finishes; short requests wait and GPU slots sit idle. Continuous batching (introduced by Orca as iteration-level scheduling) re-forms the batch at every decode step: finished sequences leave, new ones join. Large throughput gains on real traffic with mixed output lengths.

PagedAttention (vLLM)

Naively, each request reserves a contiguous KV region sized for its maximum length → internal and external fragmentation; the vLLM paper reports large waste in prior systems. PagedAttention splits KV cache into fixed-size blocks (like OS memory pages) mapped through a block table, allocated on demand. Near-zero waste → more concurrent sequences → higher throughput. Blocks can also be shared (copy-on-write) for parallel sampling and common prefixes.

Prefix caching

Many requests share a prefix (system prompt, few-shot examples, a long document). Caching the KV for that prefix skips its prefill. SGLang's RadixAttention keeps prefixes in a radix tree for automatic reuse; vLLM supports automatic prefix caching. Big win for agents with long, stable system prompts and tool definitions — order your prompt so stable parts come first.

Chunked prefill and disaggregation

A long prefill can stall everyone's decode steps (latency spikes). Chunked prefill splits prompts into chunks interleaved with decode. Prefill/decode disaggregation runs the two phases on different GPU pools because they have different bottlenecks.

The landscape

vLLM (most common open-source server), SGLang, TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA-optimised), Hugging Face TGI, plus managed endpoints. On Kubernetes: KServe or plain Deployments, ideally scaled on queue/KV metrics.

modules.lesson_html:
Quantisation

Store weights (and sometimes activations or KV cache) in fewer bits. - Weight-only INT8/INT4 — shrinks memory and speeds memory-bound decode. Methods: GPTQ (approximate second-order, layer-wise), AWQ (activation-aware: protect the small fraction of salient weights). - FP8 — on newer GPUs (e.g. H100), FP8 weights/activations with hardware support; good quality/speed trade-off. - KV cache quantisation — more concurrent sequences. Rule: quantisation is a quality change, so it must pass your evals (Pillar 4), not just perplexity. Quality loss is often uneven — check your languages (e.g. BM/Manglish) and tasks separately.

Speculative decoding

A small draft model proposes k tokens; the large target model verifies them in one forward pass. Accepted tokens are kept; on the first mismatch the target's token is used. The sampling scheme guarantees the output distribution equals the target model's — no quality loss, just speed. Helps most when the draft's acceptance rate is high and you're latency-bound at low batch sizes; gains shrink at high batch where you're compute-bound. Variants: n-gram / prompt lookup, Medusa heads, EAGLE.

FlashAttention

Standard attention materialises the full N×N attention matrix in slow GPU HBM. FlashAttention tiles the computation so blocks stay in fast on-chip SRAM, using an online softmax — exact attention with far fewer memory reads/writes. The lesson generalises: on GPUs, moving data is often the cost, not maths.

Other levers

Smaller/distilled models, shorter prompts, output length limits, structured output, routing easy requests to a small model, caching full responses for repeated questions. Often the cheapest optimisation is not in the GPU at all.

modules.lesson_html:
Benchmark correctly

  • Use a realistic distribution of input and output lengths from real or representative traffic, not one fixed prompt.
  • Sweep concurrency (1, 2, 4 … 64+) and plot throughput vs latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT). The curve's knee is your operating point.
  • Measure goodput: throughput where requests meet the SLO.
  • Warm up first; separate cold-start from steady state.
  • Tools: vLLM's benchmark scripts, NVIDIA GenAI-Perf, LLMPerf.

Cost per million tokens

cost per 1M tokens = (GPU hourly cost) / (tokens per second × 3600) × 1,000,000

Example: a GPU at $4/hour sustaining 2,000 output tokens/s at your SLO: 4 / (2,000 × 3,600) × 1,000,000 ≈ $0.56 per 1M output tokens — at 100% utilisation. At 25% average utilisation, effective cost is 4× higher (~$2.22). Utilisation is the whole game. APIs charge per token so you pay nothing when idle; self-hosting charges per hour.

Break-even thinking

Self-hosting wins when traffic is high and steady, data must stay in your environment, or you need a fine-tuned/custom model. APIs win for spiky or low traffic, frontier-quality needs, and small teams (ops cost is real: on-call, upgrades, security patching). Include engineer time in the model.

Capacity planning

Required replicas ≈ peak tokens/s ÷ per-replica goodput, plus headroom (N+1 for failure, ~30% for spikes). Scale on queue depth / in-flight requests. Consider autoscaling lag: model loading can take minutes — keep a warm minimum or use faster loading (cached weights on local NVMe).

Gateway layer

An AI gateway (APIM in your Foundry platform; LiteLLM or Envoy-based gateways elsewhere) centralises auth, quotas, token metering per team, routing, fallback between providers and caching — essential for chargeback.

modules.lesson_html:
What a platform is

The CNCF Platforms white paper defines a platform as a collection of capabilities, documentation and tools that support developing, deploying and operating products — offered as self-service and run as a product for internal users. The test of a platform is not the tech; it is whether teams choose to use it.

Team Topologies in one page

Four team types: - Stream-aligned — owns a slice of business value end to end (e.g. the pricing data science team). - Platform — provides internal services that reduce stream-aligned teams' cognitive load (your role). - Enabling — temporarily helps teams adopt new capabilities (coaching DS on MLOps practices). - Complicated-subsystem — owns a part needing deep specialist knowledge (e.g. a CV damage-detection model or an inference engine). Three interaction modes: collaboration, X-as-a-service, facilitating. A healthy platform moves from collaboration to X-as-a-service as it matures. The guiding metric is cognitive load on stream-aligned teams.

Golden paths

Spotify defines the Golden Path as "the opinionated and supported path" to build something. Key properties: optional (not mandated), opinionated, documented, supported, and kept short through templates and automation. For AI: a template that gives a new model project CI, tests, registry, deployment, monitoring and eval hooks on day one.

Measuring a platform

  • Adoption (voluntary usage rate), time-to-first-deploy for a new team.
  • DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore service.
  • Developer satisfaction surveys; support ticket volume. Your "two weeks to two days" release story is a lead-time improvement — say it in DORA language.

modules.lesson_html:
The control loop

Kubernetes is a set of controllers that continuously compare desired state (objects stored in etcd via the API server) to actual state and act to close the gap. This is level-triggered reconciliation, not one-off scripts.

kubectl apply to running pod

  1. kubectl sends the object to the API server (authn → authz/RBAC → admission controllers, including mutating and validating webhooks).
  2. Object persisted in etcd.
  3. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates Pods.
  4. The scheduler picks a node for each unscheduled Pod (filtering, then scoring), writes the binding.
  5. The kubelet on that node sees the Pod, asks the container runtime (via CRI) to pull images and start containers, sets up networking (CNI) and volumes (CSI), and reports status.

Operators and CRDs

A CustomResourceDefinition adds a new API type; an operator is a custom controller that reconciles it using domain knowledge (e.g. KServe's InferenceService, the NVIDIA GPU Operator). This is how ML platforms extend Kubernetes.

Resources and QoS

  • Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits cap usage.
  • CPU over limit → throttled. Memory over limit → OOMKilled.
  • QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests = limits for all containers), Burstable, BestEffort (none set; evicted first).

Autoscaling

  • HPA scales replicas on metrics (CPU, custom metrics like queue depth).
  • VPA adjusts requests.
  • Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter add or remove nodes when pods can't schedule.
  • KEDA scales on event sources and can scale to zero. For LLM serving, CPU is a poor scaling signal — use queue length, in-flight requests or KV-cache utilisation (Pillar 3).

modules.lesson_html:
How GPUs reach a Pod

GPUs are extended resources advertised by a device plugin (e.g. nvidia.com/gpu). Pods request them in limits; GPUs are not overcommitted — a requested GPU is exclusively assigned by default. The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs and manages the drivers, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM monitoring and MIG manager as Kubernetes-managed components.

Sharing a GPU

  • MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) — on supported data-centre GPUs (e.g. A100, H100), hardware-partitions one GPU into isolated instances with dedicated memory and compute. Strong isolation; fixed profiles.
  • Time-slicing — multiple Pods share a GPU by taking turns. No memory isolation; one tenant can OOM others. Fine for dev, notebooks, light inference.
  • MPS — concurrent processes share a GPU with better utilisation than time-slicing; limited isolation.
  • Dedicated — whole GPUs for training or large LLM serving.

Multi-tenancy

Soft multi-tenancy (trusted internal teams) usually means one namespace per team or workload with: ResourceQuota (including GPU counts), LimitRange, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, and separate node pools via taints/tolerations and node affinity for GPU nodes. Hard multi-tenancy (untrusted tenants) usually needs separate clusters or strong sandboxing.

Batch and fair-share

The default scheduler places Pods one at a time; distributed training needs gang scheduling (all workers or none). Kueue adds job queueing, quotas per queue, borrowing between teams, and preemption on top of the standard scheduler. Volcano is an alternative batch scheduler.

Cost

GPUs dominate AI platform cost. Track utilisation via DCGM metrics; idle reserved GPUs are the biggest waste. Scale-to-zero for spiky inference, spot nodes for fault-tolerant training.

modules.lesson_html:
Terraform structure

  • Modules are reusable building blocks (e.g. a "foundry-workload" module).
  • Root modules per environment/workload compose modules.
  • Remote state with locking; one state per blast-radius unit (don't put all environments in one state).
  • Pin provider and module versions; run plan in CI and require review on apply.
  • Detect drift (resources changed outside Terraform) with scheduled plans.

GitOps

GitOps (OpenGitOps principles): desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable in git, pulled automatically by agents, and continuously reconciled. Argo CD runs in the cluster, watches git, and syncs manifests — the same control-loop idea as Kubernetes itself. Benefits: audit trail, rollback via git revert, no CI system holding cluster-admin credentials. Typical split: Terraform for cloud resources (clusters, networks, identities), GitOps for in-cluster resources.

Policy as code

Admission controllers enforce rules at the API server: - Kyverno — policies written as Kubernetes YAML; validate, mutate, generate, verify images. - OPA Gatekeeper — policies in Rego via ConstraintTemplates. Example AI-platform guardrails: no containers without resource limits; GPU pods only in approved namespaces; images only from your registry and signed; no public LoadBalancers; required labels for cost allocation (team, model). Also run the same policies in CI (shift-left) so developers see failures before deploying.

Secrets and identity

Prefer workload identity (Azure Workload Identity, IRSA on AWS) over static secrets. You already used workload identity federation for Foundry agents — that's the pattern.

modules.lesson_html:
NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, 2023)

Voluntary US framework. Four functions: - Govern — culture, policies, roles, accountability (cross-cutting). - Map — understand context, intended use, stakeholders, risks. - Measure — assess and track risks with metrics (evals live here). - Manage — prioritise, respond to, and monitor risks. It also describes characteristics of trustworthy AI: valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed. The Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, 2024) applies the RMF to GenAI and lists GenAI-specific risks such as confabulation, information integrity, information security, harmful bias, data privacy and IP.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023

The first international management system standard for AI — like ISO 27001 but for AI. It specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI management system (AIMS): policy, roles, risk assessment, AI impact assessment, controls (Annex A), monitoring, internal audit, management review. It is certifiable, which is why enterprises and vendors care.

Risk tiering — the practical bridge

Not every use case needs the same controls. A tiering scheme uses criteria like: impact on individuals' rights or finances, autonomy (advice vs action), audience (internal vs public), reversibility, data sensitivity, and scale. Example: - Tier 1 (low) — internal productivity, human reviews all outputs. Controls: basic evals, logging. - Tier 2 (medium) — customer-facing information (auction assistant). Adds: eval gate, guardrails, monitoring, incident process, agent card. - Tier 3 (high) — decisions affecting people's money or rights (credit, hiring) or autonomous actions. Adds: human oversight, bias testing, independent review, sign-off, audit trail. The platform's job: make Tier-2 controls the default golden path.

modules.lesson_html:
EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

Risk-based: - Prohibited practices (e.g. social scoring, certain manipulative or exploitative systems, untargeted facial-image scraping) — banned since February 2025. - High-risk systems — Annex III use cases (e.g. employment, education, credit scoring, critical infrastructure, law enforcement) and AI in regulated products (Annex I). Obligations: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy/robustness, conformity assessment, registration. - Transparency obligations (Article 50) — e.g. telling people they're interacting with AI, marking AI-generated content. - General-purpose AI (GPAI) models — obligations for model providers since August 2025, extra duties for systemic-risk models. Timeline update: the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI postponed high-risk obligations — to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I product-embedded systems. Regulation changes; always check the current text before advising. Extraterritorial reach: it applies to providers placing AI on the EU market and to providers/deployers outside the EU when the system's output is used in the EU.

Malaysia — National Guidelines on AI Governance & Ethics (AIGE)

Launched by MOSTI on 20 September 2024. Voluntary. Seven principles (fairness; reliability, safety and control; privacy and security; inclusiveness; transparency; accountability; pursuit of human benefit and happiness) with guidance for three stakeholder groups: end users, policymakers, and developers/technology providers. Malaysia's PDPA still applies to personal data. Watch the National AI Office and the National AI Action Plan 2026–2030 for what comes next.

Singapore — Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI (2024)

From IMDA and the AI Verify Foundation; voluntary; nine dimensions: accountability, data, trusted development and deployment, incident reporting, testing and assurance, security, content provenance, safety and alignment R&D, and AI for public good. AI Verify offers testing tools — practical reference for regional companies.

How to use this as an engineer

You don't need to be a lawyer. You need to (1) classify the use case, (2) know which obligations attach, and (3) implement them as platform controls with evidence. Get legal to confirm classification.

modules.lesson_html:
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)

LLM01 Prompt Injection · LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure · LLM03 Supply Chain · LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning · LLM05 Improper Output Handling · LLM06 Excessive Agency · LLM07 System Prompt Leakage · LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses · LLM09 Misinformation · LLM10 Unbounded Consumption.

Prompt injection

  • Direct — the user types instructions to override the system.
  • Indirect — instructions hidden in content the model reads: web pages, emails, documents, tool outputs (Greshake et al., 2023). For agents this is the big one: any data source becomes an attack surface. There is no complete fix today. Defence in depth:
  • Least privilege — tools with minimal scopes; read-only by default.
  • Human confirmation for consequential actions (payments, emails, deletes).
  • Separate trusted instructions from untrusted data; never let untrusted content choose which tools to call with high-privilege arguments.
  • Output handling — treat model output as untrusted input to downstream systems (escape, validate against schemas, never eval).
  • Detection classifiers and monitoring — helpful, not sufficient. A useful rule of thumb (Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta"): danger is highest when an agent has access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. Remove one leg.

Excessive agency

Too much functionality, permission or autonomy. Fix with narrow tools, scoped identities (workload identity per agent), rate limits and approvals.

Unbounded consumption

Token floods and runaway agent loops cost money. Gateway quotas, max steps, max tokens and budget alerts per team.

MITRE ATLAS

A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on ATT&CK — useful for red-team planning.

modules.lesson_html:
Documentation artefacts

  • Model cards (Mitchell et al., 2019) — intended use, out-of-scope use, training data summary, evaluation results disaggregated by relevant groups, ethical considerations, caveats.
  • Datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al., 2018) — motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution, maintenance.
  • Agent/system cards — for LLM systems: purpose, model(s) and versions, tools and their permissions, data accessed, guardrails, eval results by slice, known limitations, owner, risk tier, escalation path. Generate as much as possible from the platform (registry metadata, eval runs) so cards don't rot.

Lineage and audit trails

For any decision you should be able to answer: which model version, which prompt version, which data/features, which tools were called with what arguments, who approved the release, and what the user saw. Pieces: model registry with lineage to data and code commit; versioned prompts; trace logs with retention policy; release approvals recorded in CI.

Human oversight that actually works

"Human in the loop" fails when reviewers rubber-stamp (automation bias). Make it meaningful: - Review only where it matters (risk-based sampling, low-confidence cases, consequential actions). - Show the reviewer the evidence (sources, tool calls), not just the answer. - Measure reviewer agreement and overturn rates; if overturns are ~0%, either the system is perfect or the review is theatre. - Clear authority to stop or roll back the system.

Incident management for AI

Define what counts as an AI incident (harmful output, data leak, major quality regression), severity levels, who is paged, how to disable a feature (kill switch / feature flag), and how incidents feed back into evals.

modules.lesson_html:
Design docs

Google-style design docs capture context and scope, goals and non-goals, the proposed design, alternatives considered, and cross-cutting concerns (security, privacy, cost, observability). Their main value is surfacing disagreement early and recording why. Keep them as short as the decision allows; a doc nobody reads didn't help.

ADRs

Michael Nygard's Architecture Decision Record: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences. One decision per record, immutable once accepted (supersede, don't edit). You already use ADRs — make "Consequences" honest, including the downsides you accept.

Public posts

What works for practitioner writing: - One idea per post, with evidence from real work (numbers, diagrams, code). - Write what you just learned — "TIL"-style posts are valuable and quick. - Show the failure, not only the success. - Title says the takeaway. - Never invent results; anonymise company data. Simon Willison's advice: write about things you've done and learned; a short post published beats a long one in drafts.

Your pipeline

Every module's exercises produce material. Convert each pillar capstone into a post on ammaradam.dev, then a short LinkedIn version linking to it.

modules.lesson_html:
Where to speak (ladder)

Local meetups (PyData KL, Kubernetes/CNCF KL, GDG, AWS/Azure user groups) → PyCon MY / regional conferences (PyCon APAC, KubeCon + CloudNativeCon events, MLOps-focused conferences) → global conferences. You've spoken at PyCon Malaysia — you're already on the ladder.

Writing a CFP that works

Reviewers read hundreds. Make theirs easy: - Title — specific, promises a takeaway ("What 100 agent traces taught us about evals in Manglish"). - Abstract — problem, why it matters, what you'll show, what attendees leave with. Concrete beats clever. - Audience and level stated clearly. - Evidence you can deliver — real system, real numbers, links to prior talks or posts. - Original material: talks about your own production experience beat survey talks.

Structuring a 25-minute talk

  1. Hook: the problem in one story (2 min).
  2. Context: just enough background (3 min).
  3. 3 key points max, each with evidence or a demo (15 min).
  4. What to do Monday morning (3 min).
  5. Resources slide (2 min). Rehearse out loud at least three times; time it; cut 20%.

Reuse

One body of work → blog post → meetup talk → conference talk → video → posts.

modules.lesson_html:
Your own project: MLOps-Toolbox

Adoption depends less on code quality than on: a README that explains the problem in one paragraph, a 5-minute quickstart, a realistic demo (PriceCatcher), clear contribution guide, tagged releases, and issues labelled "good first issue". Write the docs for a stranger.

Upstream contributions

Start with docs and small fixes in projects you use (vLLM, Feast, Kueue, OpenTelemetry, Langfuse, Evidently). Steps: read CONTRIBUTING, find a well-scoped issue, comment before starting, keep the PR small, include tests, respond to review quickly. One merged PR in a well-known project carries real signal.

Small finished things beat big unfinished ones

A published eval dataset, a tiny CLI, a Kubernetes manifest example, a benchmark notebook — each is shareable proof. Your side-project list is long; choose open-source work that reinforces your expertise story (platform + evals + Malaysia) and pause the rest.

modules.lesson_html:
Staff archetypes (Will Larson)

  • Tech Lead — guides one team's approach and execution.
  • Architect — direction and quality across a critical area.
  • Solver — parachutes into hard problems.
  • Right Hand — extends an executive's leadership across the org. Your current role (platform direction, governance, coaching DS) mixes Tech Lead and Architect.

Staff work (Tanya Reilly's framing)

Three pillars: big-picture thinking (strategy, vision, technical direction), project execution (leading hard, ambiguous projects to done), and levelling up others (mentoring, setting standards, reviews). Much of it is "glue work" — make it visible and tie it to outcomes.

Influence tools

  • Written strategy and vision docs (connect to p6m1).
  • Getting sponsors: managers and execs who will spend capital on your ideas.
  • Being "in the room" — and earning it by bringing data.
  • Making others successful (coaching DS to "drive on the roads").

IC vs manager

Managers own people outcomes (hiring, performance, growth); staff ICs own technical outcomes across teams. Both lead. Look at your energy: do you prefer 1:1s and growing people, or deep technical direction? Your coaching + visionary style fits either; the job you pick should match what you want to spend most days doing.
